old.name: Girona Cathedral (Santa Maria)
old.hook: The widest doubt in Gothic engineering, resolved in stone.
old.text: A single Gothic nave 22.98 m wide, 35 m high — the widest Gothic nave in the world, second among all church naves only to St Peter's in Rome. The exterior staircase is 90 steps, Baroque, built 1607. In Game of Thrones (filmed here September 2015) Jaime Lannister rides his horse up those steps to the Great Sept of Baelor.

old.name: Basílica de Sant Feliu
old.hook: The pre-cathedral church with eight Roman tombs in its walls.
old.text: Girona's principal church before the Cathedral, over the martyr St Felix (d. 304). A Romanesque core under a Gothic nave and Baroque façade, raised to minor basilica by Benedict XVI in 2011. Set into the presbytery are eight 3rd–4th-c. Roman and early-Christian sarcophagi, a run unique on the Iberian Peninsula.

old.name: Sant Pere de Galligants
old.hook: A Romanesque monastery that is now Catalonia's archaeology museum in Girona.
old.text: First documented 988, the present Benedictine church built in the first half of the 12th century, with a Lombard-banded octagonal tower. Since 1857 a museum; today the Girona seat of the Museu d'Arqueologia de Catalunya, holding the 4th-c. Sepulcre de les Estacions from Empúries. Its cloister played Oldtown's Citadel in Game of Thrones.

old.name: Museu d'Història dels Jueus (Call)
old.hook: Eleven rooms of a medieval Jewish world, on its own ground.
old.text: In the Centre Bonastruc ça Porta on Carrer de la Força, at the heart of the Call. Eleven rooms trace the daily life, learning and expulsion of Girona's Jewish community — the first Kabbalah school in Spain, founded around Nachmanides in the 13th century. Excavations here reached the medieval yeshiva.

old.name: Banys Àrabs
old.hook: 'Arab baths' that are actually 12th-century Christian Romanesque.
old.text: Despite the name, a Romanesque bathhouse of about 1194 modelled on Roman and Islamic precedents, not built by Muslim hands. The domed, columned central pool room (apodyterium) is the photograph everyone takes. A rare civil building of its age.

old.name: Casa Masó
old.hook: The only Onyar riverfront house you can walk into.
old.text: Birthplace of the Noucentista architect Rafael Masó (1880–1935) and the single riverside house open to visitors — four dwellings merged, the façade reworked by Masó between 1911 and 1919. Guided tours only, small groups, booking required; city-owned since 2006 and run by the Fundació Rafael Masó.

old.name: Ceramics — La Bisbal d'Empordà
old.hook: Catalonia's pottery capital, where you can still take the wheel from a named master.
old.text: La Bisbal has thrown terracotta since the Middle Ages — the clay is in the ground and the town is built on it, with a working Terracotta museum and a live ceramicists' association. The Escola de Ceràmica de la Bisbal (founded ~1972) teaches on real kilns; its summer courses run weekly from late June to early September under named masters — Dolors Ros on wheel technique, Anna Martínez on the introduction to throwing, María Torné on porcelain — at around EUR 170 a course, booked online and open to anyone. Independent ateliers in town and nearby Peratallada run shorter bookable wheel sessions too.

old.name: Ratafia — Santa Coloma de Farners
old.hook: Macerate green walnuts into the Empordà's herb liqueur, with the cooperative that revived it.
old.text: Ratafia — the EU-protected green-walnut-and-herb liqueur — has its cultural capital at Santa Coloma de Farners, and since 2021 its first dedicated obrador: La Sobirana, a young cooperative (Ernest Morell, Pau Pujol, Pau Torra) working from an 1842 tavern-keeper's recipe. Their taller d'elaboració de ratafia is a public, bookable three-hour workshop, about EUR 50 a head — the green walnuts, herbs and alcohol for two litres included — and you leave with your own maceration to age.

old.name: Cafè Le Bistrot
old.text: Unchanged in spirit since the late 1970s: a Parisian-brasserie interior at the foot of the Pujada de Sant Domènec, the terrace stacked table-by-table up the stone steps opposite the Agullana Palace — here the design pedigree is Girona's own fabric. Daily 13:00 to around midnight (2026 listings); Time Out files it under 'open until late' — kitchen hours narrower than door hours, check ahead

old.name: Palau Fugit — Gipsy bar & El Terrat
old.hook: Barri Vell (Carrer Bonaventura Carreras i Peralta, 4)
old.text: El Equipo Creativo (interiors) with Isern Associats (architecture) resurrected the long-abandoned 18th-century Baroque palace Casa Heras de Puig as a 24-room hotel in 2023: a custom Yves Klein-blue reception table under a golden chandelier against original stone, a palette lifted from the Onyar riverside façades and the Temps de Flors festival, custom nanimarquina rugs underfoot and Frederic Amat's near-three-metre ceramic fountain, Font de Garotes, in the courtyard. Casa Heras serves breakfast, lunch and dinner, bookable by non-residents via the restaurant's online module; Gipsy and El Terrat hours unpublished — call ahead

old.text: Ayla Kellens — a jewellery designer by training — shaped the interior herself and hangs her own Costa Brava canvases, for sale, in this small square-side room opened at the end of 2022 with partner Jacob, a decade-deep coffee professional who ran his own roastery in Antwerp and now roasts under his Ambient label; café, natural-wine bar, record shop and gallery sharing one space.
